episode_title: What AI Can't Replace: Leadership, Change, and the Human Side of Retail

real_qa.q: What is the biggest impediment to AI adoption according to research by Dr. Janet Sherlock and Rob Garf?
real_qa.r: According to a joint study released by Dr. Janet Sherlock and Rob Garf, the biggest impediment to AI adoption was the team's ability to change rapidly and to learn rapidly. Companies that focus on change management and help their teams become agile and resilient through change are the ones that will be successful.
real_qa.requete: Janet Sherlock Rob Garf AI adoption impediment study

real_qa.q: What was the core experience that shaped Dave Finnegan's perspective on AI and human connection at Build-A-Bear?
real_qa.r: At Build-A-Bear's Store of the Future opening with a four to four and a half hour wait, Dave witnessed a store associate kneel down to a 10-year-old girl named Grace, ask why she was there, and when she said it was her birthday, the associate rang a bell to announce her birthday to everyone in the store. This created an explosion of emotion for the child and her family, demonstrating that the highest guest satisfaction came from human connection, not technology.
real_qa.requete: Build-A-Bear Store of the Future Grace birthday bell

real_qa.q: What are the key building blocks that Olympic rugby team members used to rapidly learn and succeed despite having no prior rugby experience?
real_qa.r: The women's Olympic rugby team members, none of whom played rugby growing up, succeeded through clear mission definition, rapid feedback loops after every game and practice discussing what went well and what didn't, setting aside distinct time for execution versus innovation, and focusing on learning agility. Leaders who adopt these practices—clear mission, quick feedback on successes and failures, and delineated time for creative versus execution work—can help navigate AI challenges.
real_qa.requete: women's Olympic rugby team learning agility rapid feedback

real_qa.q: How is the next generation of shoppers different from previous generations in their retail behavior?
real_qa.r: The next generation are collectors of experiences—they document where they go, share it with others, and want to co-create retail experiences in stores where they can come, experience, post about it, and shape what that experience is. Unlike previous generations focused on collecting physical goods like cars, this generation prioritizes collecting and sharing experiences and expects brands to invite customer participation in experience creation.
real_qa.requete: Gen Z shoppers experience collectors retail behavior

real_qa.q: What is the main thesis of 'The Comfort Crisis' by Michael Easter according to Dave Finnegan?
real_qa.r: The Comfort Crisis found that 98% of people take the escalator over stairs even in the Olympic Village among athletes, and repeated this pattern globally. The thesis is that humans have eliminated discomfort through technology and convenience, which prevents growth and richer experiences. By reintroducing challenging and uncomfortable situations into life, people can harness discomfort's power to grow and learn more.
real_qa.requete: The Comfort Crisis Michael Easter escalator stairs study

guest.bio_context: Dave Finnegan helped build Build-A-Bear Workshop where he spent nearly 15 years heading up technology and interaction, and the store of the future concept; he went public with the company and appeared on Oprah's show. He then worked for almost a decade at Orbis, an outdoor fly fishing brand based in Vermont with guides and lodges worldwide. After a year backpacking around the planet interviewing tribes, scientists, and monks, he joined private equity at New Road and became an ambassador for the National Retail Federation, working with councils for CIOs, CMOs, and CDOs. He is currently pursuing a master's degree in anthropology.

real_quote: AI is really, really good at making things more and more convenient, but AI doesn't build relationships, it doesn't connect, and that's where the human component is really, really strong.
